name: Rose
lede: Rose is a vivid pink halfway between red and magenta, named after the flower. For most of history, though, the word meant red, and the pink we now call rose had to wait for new dyes and new garden roses to get a name of its own.

sections.title: A flower that used to be red
sections.body:
The Romans had a word built on the flower, *roseus*, but it did not mean pink [1]. It meant a bright, beautiful red, close to vermilion, and it described women's makeup and cloth dyed with kermes [1]. Homer's famous rosy-fingered dawn is the same: a red glow on the sky, not a pink flower [1][9]. Greek and Latin had no adjective for pink at all, though people plainly saw the shade in flowers, stones and sunsets [1].

The flowers themselves explain part of this. Pastoureau notes that the roses of antiquity and the Middle Ages were red, white or sometimes yellow, and almost never pink [1][2]. Pliny opened his account of flowers with the rose and the lily, and for medieval writers the rose was the red flower and the lily the white one [4]. In Rome the rose also had a solemn side: it was strewn for the dead during the Rosalia, a festival held between May and July [3].

The meaning held for a thousand years. In medieval Latin *roseus* still meant vermilion and was used for cheeks and lips, while the rare Old French adjective *rose* meant something pale, beige or yellowish rather than pink [1]. The modern sense of [[vermilion]] and the old sense of rose were close neighbors [1]. Medieval lip colors made with kermes or madder were sometimes scented with rose, and the fashion was for bright red lips against whitened cheeks [23].

The flower's meaning shifted before its color did. In late medieval images of the Virgin, Pastoureau writes, the rose began to challenge the lily: the red flower of love gained ground on the white flower of purity [24]. The rose that carried that meaning was still a red one [4][24].

sections.title: How pink got a name
sections.body:
Pink as a fashionable color began with a dye. Around 1380 to 1400, Pastoureau writes, Italian dyers found mordants that made the Asian dyewood brazilwood hold fast, producing true pinks on cloth for the first time in Europe [1]. Jean de Berry, the great collector, launched a pink craze at the French court, and painters and illuminators soon turned the same dye into a pigment [1].

The new color still needed a word. The answer came from Venetian and Tuscan *incarnato*, until then a word for the complexion, which gave French *incarnat* by about 1400 to 1420, Castilian *encarnado*, and English carnation a few decades later [1]. Placing it was harder. In the color order inherited from Aristotle, yellow already sat between white and red, so from the fifteenth to the seventeenth centuries writers and manuals treated carnation as a pale yellow, not a pale red [1].

The eighteenth century settled it. Brazilwood from South America made pink affordable, and Madame de Pompadour made it the fashion in French interiors, often paired with sky blue [1]. St Clair adds that she helped popularise bright pink Sèvres porcelain [5]. By then, Pastoureau writes, gardeners had bred truly pink roses, and the color took the flower's name: French *rose*, Spanish *rosa*, Portuguese *cor-de-rosa*, German *rosa* [1]. Even so, the French Academy's dictionary admitted *rose* as a color word only in its edition of 1835 [1].

sections.title: Rose, pink and the other languages
sections.body:
English took a different road. St Clair notes that in most languages other than English, the word for pink comes from the word for rose [6]. In English, *pink* first named a kind of pigment: a dye fixed on chalk or a similar white powder, and most often yellow [7]. There were green pinks, brown pinks, and rose pinks, and Paterson suggests the last of these slowly carried the word over to the color [9][7].

The history is visible in pigment names. Rose pink was a cheap lake of brazilwood on chalk; its earliest recorded use is in the 1729 English translation of a French painting manual, and by 1764 it was described as a rose lake used mostly for house paint and wallpaper [8]. In the seventeenth century the same thing was called roset, from a medieval Latin word meaning rose-colored [8].

English kept *rose* for the family of pinks named after the flower. Paterson lists damask, a deep pink; rose Pompadour and rose du Barry, both pinks; and tea rose, a yellowish pink that Maerz and Paul thought should be dropped because tea roses come in many colors [9]. The phrase rose-colored glasses, for an unrealistically cheerful view, rests on the same flower [9].

sections.title: What colors a rose
sections.body:
A rose is not colored the way a stone is. Rose quartz owes its pink to traces of titanium or manganese, but no metal tints a rose petal; its colorants are organic molecules made by the plant [11]. That is why the flower can be bred into new colors, and why the truly pink rose is, in Pastoureau's account, a fairly recent garden product [1].

Two effects of seeing change how roses look. By moonlight, many observers have noticed that red roses look black, because in dim light the eye's sensitivity shifts away from red [14]. And Chevreul warned that a rose red placed beside a rosy face drains its freshness and pushes it toward green [15]. A rose looks pinker against green leaves than against another pink.

sections.title: Rose in the paintbox
sections.body:
Painters made rose colors from insects, roots and woods. Schäffer's color chart of 1769 mixed its rose red from cochineal and lead white [16]. The most famous rose paint is rose madder, a pale, clear lake made by extracting only part of the coloring matter of the [[madder]] root; the colorman George Field was its best-known maker in the early nineteenth century [8][13]. Genuine rose madder is still made from roots, and the process takes more than three months [13].

Those pinks were often fugitive. Van Gogh's *[[art:nga-72328|Roses]]* in Washington was long called *White Roses*, until traces of what was probably madder red showed that the flowers had been pink and had faded [12]. Rose also named the first aniline reds: in Britain the dye later called [[magenta]] was first sold as roseine [10].

In painting, rose was a color of display. Titian's 1568 portrait of the dealer Jacopo Strada shows shining rose-colored silk sleeves against a black doublet, a sign of commercial success [17]. Early Christian apse mosaics painted dawn as rosy bands of cloud [18]. Picasso's rose period of 1905 to 1907 followed his blue period and brought brighter colors [19].

sections.title: Myths and loose ends
sections.body:
The idea that pink was always a girls' color is a myth. In the eighteenth century pink was not reserved for girls at all, and many boys wore it until late in the nineteenth century [1]. In 1918 an American trade publication called pink the stronger color and so better for boys, with blue as the daintier color for girls [5]. Pastoureau dates the firm rule of pink for girls and blue for boys to the 1930s, when fabrics that survived boiling washes made the colors practical for babies [1].

The rosy-fingered dawn and the Latin *roseus* are a translation trap rather than a myth: read as pink, they mislead [1]. Rose madder and rose doré are different names for the same madder pigment in Paterson, not colors made from roses [9].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The screen swatch, #FF0080, has a hue of exactly 330 degrees, halfway between pure red and pure magenta on the computer color wheel [20]. It is far more saturated than any rose petal or any paint in this story; its nearest ISCC-NBS category, deep purplish pink, is almost twelve units away [20]. Its closest named neighbors are [[deep-pink]] and [[french-fuchsia]] [20]. A pink this strong is closer to the twentieth century's loud pinks than to any garden flower [20]. Elsa Schiaparelli took her 'shocking' pink from a 17.47-carat pink diamond worn by the heiress Daisy Fellowes and used it to package her first perfume, Shocking, in 1937 [25]. The editor Diana Vreeland called pink "the navy blue of India" [5]. See [[hot-pink]] for that branch of the family.

Other standards picture rose very differently. The RAL chart of 1927 gives Rose as a muted coral red, #D3545F, and Werner's nomenclature, as extended by Syme, made Rose Red a carmine with much white and a little cochineal, with the common garden rose as its example [20][16]. The family runs from [[rose-red]] and [[rose-pink]] to the greyed [[old-rose]], [[dusty-rose]] and the near-white [[misty-rose]] [20].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The screen rose almost never appears in paintings. Within six units of this swatch at five per cent of the canvas, none of our 23,781 paintings qualifies, and even within twelve units at one per cent only one does: Patrick Henry Bruce's [[art:nga-166434|Peinture/Nature Morte]] of 1924 [21]. The RAL rose fares better: 14 paintings carry it, led by Matisse's [[art:commons-Q21729783|Seville Still Life]] of 1910 and Munch's *On the Sofa* of 1913 [21].

The earliest dated example of that muted rose is a Madonna and Child of about 1320 by the Master of San Torpè, and India again carries it far more often than average, with 7 of our 721 Indian paintings [21]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [21]. Van Gogh's *Roses* shows how far a painted rose can drift: as photographed today, the six main colors our archive reads in it are all greens, from pastel green to hunter green, with no pink among them [21]. The word itself cannot be traced in Google Books, because *rose* is also the past tense of *rise* [22].

questions.q: Why did the Latin word roseus mean bright red rather than pink?
choices: Ancient roses were mostly red or white, and Latin had no word for pink
Roseus came from a red mineral, not the flower
Pink roses were banned in Rome
questions.answer: Ancient roses were mostly red or white, and Latin had no word for pink

questions.q: True or false: pink has always been the color for girls.

openers: For two thousand years 'rose' meant red: the roses of Rome and the Middle Ages were red, white or yellow.
From the 1400s to the 1600s, Europe's color books filed pink as a pale shade of yellow.
